seo.title: Suzy Says Game: Command Rules and Windows Controls
seo.description: Explore the Suzy Says game, command rules, Windows controls and edition differences. Use worked examples to prepare your first run without revealing endings.

content.heading: Suzy Says game: listen before you move

blocks.text: Suzy Says is MOONBIT’s first-person horror game about a mysterious interactive DVD and its cheerful host. A colored floor mat turns spoken instructions into movement tasks: listen for the qualifying words, identify the requested action, then find its target. This guide explains the original game’s command rule and Windows controls without revealing its later story. The browser player on this page has not been verified as the original Suzy Says game.

The difficult decision often arrives before you touch a movement key. Recognizing a color tells you where a task points; it does not tell you whether to obey. Keep the host’s wording in mind while looking at the mat. A sound elsewhere in the house may draw your attention, but it does not supply the missing words of a command.

The original Windows release uses a keyboard for movement, jumping and crouching. MOONBIT also offers a separate Android app. Neither release establishes the identity or controls of an independently hosted browser frame. Use the Windows instructions below for that edition, and check the controls shown inside any other version before starting a session.

blocks.alt: Suzy appearing on the television in a purple bedroom
blocks.caption: Keep the television in view while listening to the current instruction.

blocks.text: The qualifying Suzy says words are the decision you make before choosing a destination. When the host uses those words to give an instruction, carry out the requested action. When that qualification is missing, do not perform the requested action merely because you recognize its target. The opening practice draws attention to missing qualifying words, so listen for that distinction before matching an action to the room.
Compare two example lines that name the same yellow target. Only one supplies the qualifying words. Knowing where the color is does not supply the missing permission to jump.

rows: Make the requested jump within the task timing.
The host gives the qualifying words and identifies the action and target.
Do not make that requested jump.
The target is clear, but the qualifying words are missing.

blocks.text: In the original Windows controls, WASD moves, Space jumps and C crouches. Learn what each action looks like before a crowded sequence makes you divide your attention. A jump has both a starting position and a landing position: being near a colored area is not the same as placing yourself on it. Look down briefly when the game gives you time, establish where the mat colors are, and avoid making a large corrective movement while another line is beginning.

A useful mental sequence is permission, action, place. First ask whether the line qualifies. Next identify what your body or view needs to do. Finally find the named area or object. This order prevents a common mistake: hearing green and pressing Space before noticing the missing prefix. It also helps with longer instructions, where the correct action may be easy but its target is in another part of the house.

Do not turn every pause into an opportunity to wander. Remaining attentive is an active part of the game, especially when the television host changes pace or the room provides a distraction. If a line is unclear, compare the spoken instruction with the available subtitle rather than treating a sudden visual effect as a second order. Subtitles help identify wording; they do not remove the need to decide whether the instruction counts.

blocks.alt: Four colored floor pads in front of the bedroom television in Suzy Says
blocks.caption: Locate the colored pads before matching a command to its target.

content.heading: Keep a map of the ordinary house

blocks.text: The game does more than ask you to move on a mat. Its domestic spaces make the instructions feel increasingly personal: a television, furniture, pictures and household objects become things you must notice and distinguish. Before committing to a route, connect the object name to something recognizable in the environment. The useful question is not simply which way can I walk, but what exactly did that sentence ask me to find.

Treat the room as a small set of landmarks. The television anchors your starting orientation; doorways tell you where you leave that space; distinctive household objects help you recognize an errand destination. When you return, face the game area deliberately rather than stopping at the first convenient patch of floor. A stable reference point makes the next instruction easier to interpret and reduces unnecessary camera movement.

The listening rule still matters when an instruction names something away from the starting area. A convincing household task is not automatically valid just because you know where the target is. Finish the decision before following the route. Conversely, when the game actually calls for an errand, staying on the mat and waiting for a color prompt will not complete that different task.

After a missed task, reconstruct three details: the full sentence, the action you performed and your final position. If the command lacked the qualifying words, reaching the named object was still the wrong response. If it qualified, check whether you performed its verb rather than merely finding the noun. That gives you a specific correction to make on the next instruction.

content.heading: Separate a mistake from a technical problem

blocks.text: A scare or sharp change in presentation does not by itself prove that a key failed. The game uses uncertainty to put pressure on an otherwise small control set. Before changing browser settings, remember the instruction, its prefix and your position. If you obeyed an unqualified command, that is a different problem from a movement key that never reaches the player.

For a genuine input problem, first give the game area focus with a deliberate click. Keys can otherwise scroll the surrounding webpage or operate a browser control instead of the embedded experience. If Space scrolls the page, return to the player and check focus before concluding that jumping is unavailable. Do not repeatedly press movement keys while the player is still on a loading screen.

Use the page fullscreen control when the surrounding article makes the game too small. Browser fullscreen is a separate mode and may be refused by the browser; the visible exit control remains useful even when a cross-origin game has keyboard focus. A larger view can make a mat color, subtitle or interaction target easier to identify, but it does not change the game rules.

If loading stops, use the player’s retry action rather than opening several copies at once. A failed network request, a restrictive browser setting and an in-game story event are different explanations. Keep one session in view so that audio and input are not split between tabs. Restarting may discard the current run; there is no promise here that every embedded build stores progress or resumes at the same point.

The original release separates the base download from a Full version. The Full version includes an endless mode and a secret ending; it is offered at a minimum payment of one dollar and fifty cents on the original store. A mode being part of that download does not mean the same mode is included in every browser-hosted version. Check the menu of the experience that actually loads before following mode-specific advice.

For a first visit, prepare the session before looking for ending triggers. Choose the original edition you want, make the controls and subtitles comfortable, then use the television and mat as starting landmarks. The first-run guide walks through those preparation decisions. Once an instruction is present, the command guide takes over with qualifying-word and action examples without revealing later events.

For Full’s endless mode, keep the same command-reading routine across successive tasks. For a story session, leave yourself time to follow the house and its interruptions. Match advice to the edition and mode you selected: an ending label in a recreation or a video title is not a menu option in your own copy.

blocks.caption: The DVD box introduces the game within the house.

content.heading: Make the first run easier to read

blocks.text: Use an ordinary, comfortable volume. Sound can help you follow the host, but horror audio can change abruptly, so maximum volume is unnecessary. Enable subtitles when the active version offers them and position the screen so the instruction area stays easy to read. Flashing lights, jumpscares and unsettling scenes are part of the original game’s warning; stop if those effects are uncomfortable.

On Windows, arrange the keyboard so Space and C are reachable while your other hand controls the view. Android uses its own app interface; consult its displayed controls instead of translating each Windows key into an assumed touch gesture. A phone opening this webpage does not establish that the embedded game offers the same experience as either official release.

Keep your first goal modest and concrete: recognize a valid instruction and complete it cleanly. Once that sequence feels familiar, add the room layout and longer errands. The practical advantage comes from reducing rushed decisions, not from making the game louder or moving continuously. When you want more help, choose the Guide that matches the exact point of confusion rather than reading every story detail at once.

items.question: What are the original movement controls?
items.answer: WASD moves, Space jumps and C crouches in the original Windows release. Follow the active player’s own prompts if its build differs.

items.question: Does every spoken action need a response?
items.answer: No. Listen for the qualifying Suzy says words before performing the requested action. When those words are missing, do not carry out that action.

items.question: Is the original game a browser release?
items.answer: MOONBIT offers a Windows download and a separate Android app. This page’s browser player has not been verified as the original Suzy Says game; the controls and command examples here describe the original release.

items.question: Should I read a complete ending guide first?
items.answer: The first-run guide helps with choosing an edition, preparing controls and subtitles, and recognizing the opening. Use the command guide when you need help interpreting a line without revealing later story events.
